title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Every segment of this enterprise exists to solve a different failure mode in American healthcare—from actuarial risk pooling at UnitedHealthcare to clinical delivery, claims intelligence, and pharmacy economics at Optum.
epigraph.author: Operating Architecture Synthesis, FY2025 Form 10-K & Q3 2026 Disclosures

web_blocks.title: Consolidated Revenue Architecture: UnitedHealthcare vs. Optum

web_blocks.html: UnitedHealth Group runs two complementary platforms: UnitedHealthcare (health benefits and risk-bearing insurance) and Optum (health services, care delivery, technology analytics, and pharmacy care). In the FY2025 Form 10-K, these roll up into four formal reportable segments: UnitedHealthcare, Optum Health, Optum Insight, and Optum Rx [2], [18]. In FY2025, UnitedHealthcare generated $344,939 million in revenue (+16% YoY) and $9,431 million in operating earnings (a 2.73% margin). Optum generated $270,555 million in total revenue (+7% YoY) and $9,539 million in operating earnings (a 3.53% margin) [3], [18]. Optum sells pharmacy benefit management, care delivery, and claims processing directly to UnitedHealthcare health plans. Because of that internal trade, roughly $167.9 billion of intersegment revenue is eliminated in consolidation. That leaves consolidated FY2025 revenue of $447,567 million and consolidated operating earnings of $18,964 million [18].

Through the first nine months of 2026, the profitability mix swung back toward historical balance. UnitedHealthcare shed ~1.8 million lower-margin lives and repriced its benefit plans across the book. It ended Q3 2026 with 48.3 million domestic consumers, down from 49.8 million at year-end 2025 [3], [4]. In Q3 2026 alone, UnitedHealthcare generated $86.3 billion in revenue and $2.8 billion in operating earnings (a 3.3% margin). Optum generated $66.9 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in operating earnings (a 5.5% margin). Together, they lifted consolidated 9M 2026 operating earnings to $23,544 million on $336,447 million of consolidated revenue [4], [19].

web_blocks.title: UnitedHealthcare: Three Insurance Engines with Concrete End-to-End Examples

web_blocks.html: 1. Employer & Individual ($79.2B FY2025 revenue): Serves large national corporations, mid-sized firms, small businesses, and ACA individual-exchange buyers. Concrete Example: Consider a Fortune 500 manufacturing employer with 35,000 U.S. workers facing 8% annual medical inflation and high specialty-drug spend. Instead of buying fully insured coverage, the employer hires UnitedHealthcare under an Administrative Services Only (ASO) self-funded contract. UnitedHealthcare provides access to its national Choice Plus PPO network, delivering hospital discounts of 40%–55% off billed charges. It also processes employee claims and layers on its Surest copay-only digital plan design. The employer pays a fixed Per-Employee-Per-Month (PEPM) administrative fee plus shared-savings fees on out-of-network claims, while keeping the medical risk.

2. Medicare & Retirement ($171.3B FY2025 revenue): UnitedHealthcare's largest revenue engine, delivering Medicare Advantage (Part C), Medicare Supplement (Medigap), and Part D drug plans to seniors. Concrete Example: A 71-year-old retiree in Maricopa County, Arizona, has Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. She enrolls in an AARP-branded UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage PPO plan with a $0 monthly plan premium beyond her standard Part B premium. CMS pays UnitedHealthcare a monthly capitated base rate adjusted by her county benchmark, her HCC risk score under CMS V28, and the plan's Star Rating bonus (a 5% bonus for 4+ star plans). In return, UnitedHealthcare covers her hospital, physician, Part D drug, dental, and vision benefits. The plan also deploys in-home HouseCalls nurse-practitioner visits to close care gaps and document chronic conditions.

3. Community & State ($94.4B FY2025 revenue): Contracts with state Medicaid agencies to manage care for low-income families, pregnant women, and dual-eligible (Medicare + Medicaid) adults with complex needs. Concrete Example: A state Medicaid agency awards UnitedHealthcare a multi-year contract covering 450,000 members, including high-need dual-eligible adults. A 58-year-old member with heart failure and unstable housing gets a dedicated care coordinator. The coordinator books non-emergency rides to heart clinic visits and links the member to local food aid, preventing $18,000 emergency-room readmissions. The state pays UnitedHealthcare an actuarially certified Per-Member-Per-Month (PMPM) capitation rate, subject to state MLR corridors (typically 85%–89%).

web_blocks.title: Optum: Three Health-Services Engines with Concrete End-to-End Examples

web_blocks.html: 4. Optum Health ($101.2B FY2025 revenue; $(278)M FY2025 operating loss): Operates primary, specialty, urgent, ambulatory-surgery (SCA Health), behavioral, and home-health (LHC Group, Amedisys) care delivery networks. The unit serves ~100+ million consumers overall and ~4.7 million patients in fully accountable value-based care models [22]. Concrete Example: A 76-year-old Medicare Advantage member in Florida is attributed to an Optum Care primary-care clinic under a global capitation contract. Instead of billing fee-for-service per visit, Optum Health receives ~80%–85% of the member's CMS monthly premium up front. When the patient gets a knee replacement at an Optum-owned Surgical Care Affiliates (SCA) surgery center ($12,000 episode cost vs. $28,000 in a hospital ward) and recovers at home with an LHC Group physical therapist instead of a skilled nursing facility, Optum Health captures the clinical savings. However, if senior inpatient and outpatient care use exceeds the capitated budget, as happened in 2025, Optum Health absorbs the loss directly.

5. Optum Insight ($19.2B FY2025 revenue; $2,624M FY2025 operating earnings): Provides revenue-cycle management, claims clearinghouse links (via Change Healthcare), payment-integrity auditing, and AI clinical analytics to hospitals, health systems, and payers. The unit is backed by a $31B–$33B contract backlog [3], [18]. Concrete Example: A 12-hospital regional health system struggles with 11% claim-denial rates and 52 days in accounts receivable. It signs a 7-year managed revenue-cycle and analytics contract with Optum Insight. Optum Insight embeds its clearinghouse EDI pipes and AI prior-authorization and coding software inside the hospital's EHR workflow. The tools catch missing clinical notes before claims leave the building and audit payer underpayments. The health system pays Optum Insight a multi-year SaaS subscription plus a percentage of net cash collected above baseline.

6. Optum Rx ($151.3B FY2025 revenue; $7,193M FY2025 operating earnings): Processes over 1.52 billion adjusted prescriptions annually (>400 million per quarter) through retail pharmacy networks, Genoa behavioral pharmacies, and Optum Specialty/Home Delivery [3], [18]. Concrete Example: A large municipal school district with 25,000 covered lives contracts with Optum Rx to manage its pharmacy benefit. When a teacher is prescribed a $1,000/month GLP-1 or $6,000/month immunology biologic, Optum Rx routes the script through its formulary engine and negotiates drugmaker rebates. Under its 2025–2026 transparent pass-through contracts, it passes 100% of those rebates back to the client [23]. Optum Specialty Pharmacy then ships the biologic via cold-chain home delivery with nurse adherence coaching, earning per-claim admin fees, dispensing margins, and specialty-pharmacy spread.

web_blocks.title: Intersegment Economics and the 2026 Portfolio Pruning

web_blocks.html: Reading UnitedHealth Group's segment numbers requires tracking the $167.9 billion intersegment elimination line in FY2025 [18]. UnitedHealthcare buys pharmacy management from Optum Rx, claims analytics from Optum Insight, and clinical care from Optum Health. As a result, roughly 62% of Optum's $270.6 billion gross revenue comes from sister UnitedHealthcare plans [3], [18]. Even so, Optum also serves over 100 outside health plans, thousands of hospitals, and large self-insured employers directly. That external client base gives Optum real commercial validation beyond its captive UnitedHealthcare book [4].

In 2026, management pruned both platforms to restore unit profits. At UnitedHealthcare, domestic membership fell by ~1.8 million lives YoY to 48.3 million at Q3 2026. That drop reflects planned Medicare Advantage county exits, ACA individual-exchange repricing, and ongoing state Medicaid redeterminations [4]. At Optum Health, management sold its remaining South American units and exited losing third-party value-based care contracts where coding math failed hurdle rates. Capital now focuses on core U.S. clinics, SCA Health surgery centers, and home-health integration after the December 2025 Amedisys close [12], [22].

book_paragraphs: To make sense of a company that collects nearly $450 billion in annual revenue, you and I have to strip away the corporate org chart and follow a single healthcare dollar from the moment an employer or government agency writes a check to the moment a doctor, hospital, or pharmacist gets paid. UnitedHealth Group is built on two massive pillars—UnitedHealthcare and Optum—that intersect so deeply that roughly $168 billion of Optum's $270.6 billion in FY2025 revenue came from serving UnitedHealthcare itself.

Start on the insurance side at UnitedHealthcare, which generated $344.9 billion in FY2025 revenue across three distinct customer engines. The first is Employer & Individual, a $79.2 billion business. Imagine a 35,000-employee national manufacturer watching its medical costs climb 8% a year. Instead of buying a traditional fully insured policy, that manufacturer hires UnitedHealthcare on an Administrative Services Only contract. The manufacturer keeps the medical risk on its own balance sheet and pays UnitedHealthcare a predictable per-employee-per-month fee to plug into the Choice Plus PPO network—securing 40% to 55% hospital discounts—and to deploy digital copay-only plans like Surest that steer workers toward lower-cost, higher-quality providers.

The second and largest insurance engine is Medicare & Retirement, which generated $171.3 billion in FY2025. Picture a 71-year-old retiree in Phoenix living with diabetes and hypertension who enrolls in an AARP-branded UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan for a $0 monthly plan premium. Every month, CMS wires UnitedHealthcare a risk-adjusted capitation payment based on her county benchmark, her chronic-condition HCC risk score, and the plan's Star Rating bonus. In exchange, UnitedHealthcare pays her hospital, doctor, and Part D drug bills, sending HouseCalls nurse practitioners into her home to catch health risks early and keep her out of the emergency room.

The third insurance engine is Community & State, a $94.4 billion Medicaid business. Picture a state Medicaid agency hiring UnitedHealthcare to manage 450,000 low-income and dual-eligible residents. When a 58-year-old member with congestive heart failure lacks reliable transit to his cardiologist, a UnitedHealthcare care coordinator arranges rides and food support—preventing an $18,000 hospital readmission—while the state pays an actuarially certified monthly capitation rate.

Now cross the hallway into Optum, where the unregulated services magic—and recently, the execution pain—lives. Optum Health is a $101.2 billion care-delivery network employing or affiliating with tens of thousands of clinicians and caring for 4.7 million patients in fully accountable value-based care contracts. Picture a 76-year-old senior in Florida whose Optum Care clinic takes global capitation risk: Optum receives roughly 80% to 85% of the CMS premium up front. If that senior needs a knee replacement, Optum routes him to its own Surgical Care Affiliates ambulatory center for $12,000 instead of a $28,000 hospital inpatient stay, and sends an LHC Group physical therapist to his home. When clinical execution works, Optum captures the spread. When senior utilization spikes faster than expected—as happened in 2025—Optum Health eats the loss, which is why it posted a $(278) million operating loss in FY2025 before pruning contracts in 2026.

Next is Optum Insight, a $19.2 billion health-technology and revenue-cycle powerhouse with a $31 billion to $33 billion contract backlog. Imagine a 12-hospital regional health system losing millions to 11% claim-denial rates. Optum Insight embeds its clearinghouse pipes and AI coding software directly into the hospital's electronic health record, catching billing errors before submission and taking a recurring SaaS fee plus a slice of recovered revenue.

Finally, there is Optum Rx, the $151.3 billion pharmacy benefit manager that generated $7.19 billion of operating earnings in FY2025 and processes over 1.52 billion adjusted prescriptions a year. When a school district's teacher is prescribed a $6,000-a-month biologic, Optum Rx negotiates the manufacturer rebate—increasingly passing 100% of rebates back to the employer under 2026 transparency contracts—and ships the temperature-controlled medication directly from Optum Specialty Pharmacy with nurse coaching. Together, those six concrete loops explain why UnitedHealth Group touches more than 120 million Americans—and why a breakdown in any single link ripples across the entire P&L.

Before we leave the segment tour, you and I should look closely at how the two halves of UnitedHealth Group interact—and why management spent 2026 trimming the edges of both. Roughly 62% of Optum's $270.6 billion gross revenue comes from serving UnitedHealthcare itself, which is why $167.9 billion disappears in intersegment eliminations on the consolidated income statement. Yet the remaining 38%—over $100 billion of external business—comes from rival health plans, regional hospital systems, and Fortune 500 employers who hire Optum Rx, Optum Insight, or Optum Health on their own merits.

In 2026, CEO Stephen Hemsley and Optum chief Dr. Patrick Conway drew a sharp line between core domestic compounding and empire-building bloat. They exited South American care-delivery assets that had dragged on Optum Health returns, pruned unprofitable third-party value-based care contracts, and allowed UnitedHealthcare's total domestic membership to step down from 49.8 million to 48.3 million lives. Shrinking revenue by 0.4% in Q3 2026 while growing operating earnings 52% to $6.6 billion is the clearest proof yet that mix quality matters far more than raw headcount.

book_callouts.label: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.title: Following the Intersegment Dollar
book_callouts.text: On paper, UnitedHealthcare and Optum sum to $615.5 billion of FY2025 segment revenue, yet consolidated revenue is $447.6 billion. That $167.9 billion elimination is the beating heart of the enterprise: UnitedHealthcare is Optum's largest customer, which means Optum's margins are partly a transfer of value out of regulated insurance into unregulated services.
